section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Harmonic Series
section_1.content: Introduce the series 1/n^s. Explain that when s=1, the series diverges (the harmonic series). We use this as a baseline to understand how changing 's' alters the 'speed' at which terms shrink.
section_1.example: Visual of a pile of books: if you keep stacking them, a harmonic series grows to infinity, but changing 's' makes the pile finite.

section_2.title: Defining the Riemann Zeta Function
section_2.content: Define ζ(s) = Σ (1/n^s) for Re(s) > 1. Use an animation showing the plot of the function on the complex plane, transitioning from real numbers to complex inputs.
section_2.example: A 'Number Factory': Input 's' (a value), and the machine outputs a point on the complex plane. Watch as different 's' values map to distinct, elegant coordinate positions.

section_3.title: The Bridge: The Euler Product Formula
section_3.content: Present the identity relating the sum to prime numbers: ζ(s) = Π (1 / (1 - p^-s)). Explain that this connects the smooth world of analysis (functions) to the jagged world of primes.
section_3.example: A filter system: Imagine a sieve where each prime number 'p' acts as a gatekeeper, refining the input to reveal the hidden structure of the integers.

section_4.title: The Mystery: Analytic Continuation & The Critical Strip
section_4.content: Briefly explain 'Analytic Continuation' (extending the function to other values of s). Highlight the 'Critical Strip' (0 < Re(s) < 1) where the function behaves chaotically, leading to the Riemann Hypothesis.
section_4.example: A treasure map: The function is like a map; we have a small piece, and analytic continuation is the process of unfolding the rest of the map to reveal the location of 'zeros'.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Why it Matters
section_5.content: Summarize the significance: If all non-trivial zeros lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2, it reveals the 'harmonic' distribution of prime numbers. Final teaser: The Millennium Prize Problem.
section_5.example: The 'Prime Orchestra': Explain that if the hypothesis is true, prime numbers aren't just random static—they are notes in a beautifully tuned, complex symphony.
